Below is a draft policy section you could adapt for a university handbook, followed by a practical enforcement model for a lecturer teaching a 200-student course.

---

# Academic Integrity Policy: Use of AI Tools by Students

## 1. Purpose
The university recognizes that AI tools may support learning when used responsibly. At the same time, unapproved AI use may compromise academic integrity, originality, privacy, and fair assessment. This policy establishes permitted, restricted, and prohibited uses of AI tools by students.

## 2. Definition of AI Tools
For purposes of this policy, “AI tools” include generative and predictive systems that can produce, modify, translate, summarize, analyze, or infer content, such as text, images, code, audio, video, or data outputs. Examples include chatbots, writing assistants, translation tools, coding assistants, summarizers, and image generators.

## 3. General Principle
Students remain fully responsible for all submitted work, including any AI-assisted content. Use of AI does not transfer authorship, accountability, or academic responsibility to the tool.

---

# 4. Permitted Uses
Unless a course syllabus or assessment instruction states otherwise, the following uses are permitted:

### 4.1 Learning Support
Students may use AI tools for:
- brainstorming topics or outlines
- explaining concepts, formulas, or procedures
- generating practice questions or quizzes
- checking grammar, spelling, and style
- translating for comprehension purposes
- summarizing readings for personal study
- debugging code or understanding programming concepts

### 4.2 Administrative and Non-graded Tasks
Students may use AI tools for:
- organizing schedules or study plans
- generating personal study notes from their own materials
- formatting references, provided the final references are checked for accuracy
- creating drafts of emails or administrative messages

### 4.3 Low-stakes Practice
Students may use AI tools in practice exercises, drafts, or simulations that are explicitly labeled as practice and not submitted for grading.

### 4.4 Disclosure Requirement
Where AI use is permitted, students must disclose:
- the tool used
- the purpose of use
- the extent of AI assistance
- any prompt or output that materially influenced the submitted work, if requested by the lecturer

---

# 5. Restricted Uses
The following uses are restricted and may only be used if the lecturer or course syllabus explicitly allows them:

### 5.1 Drafting of Assessed Work
AI may not be used to generate substantial portions of essays, reports, reflections, case analyses, or presentations unless specifically authorized.

### 5.2 Code and Technical Assignments
AI-assisted coding, problem solving, or data analysis is restricted unless the instructor allows it and the student documents how AI was used.

### 5.3 Translation and Paraphrasing
AI tools may not be used to translate or paraphrase assessed work in a way that conceals the student’s own language ability or source use, unless approved.

### 5.4 Use of AI in Group Work
In group assignments, AI use must be agreed upon by all group members and disclosed in the submission. One member may not introduce undisclosed AI content on behalf of the group.

### 5.5 Use of AI on Course Materials
Students may not upload copyrighted lecture notes, exams, assignment prompts, or unpublished course materials into third-party AI systems if this violates university policy, instructor instructions, or data protection requirements.

### 5.6 Sensitive or Personal Data
Students may not enter personal data, confidential research data, patient information, or other sensitive information into AI tools without authorization.

---

# 6. Prohibited Uses
The following uses constitute academic misconduct:

### 6.1 Submitting AI-Generated Work as One’s Own
Students may not submit AI-generated text, answers, code, images, graphs, or other outputs as if they were entirely their own work when this has not been authorized.

### 6.2 Ghostwriting
Students may not use AI to produce complete assignments, exam answers, theses, or project reports for submission.

### 6.3 Misrepresentation
Students may not falsely claim that work was independently produced when AI was used in a way that should have been disclosed.

### 6.4 Unauthorized Use in Examinations
Students may not use AI tools during quizzes, tests, midterms, finals, take-home exams, or timed assessments unless the lecturer explicitly permits it.

### 6.5 Fabrication and Hallucination
Students may not submit AI-generated citations, quotations, references, data, case law, statistics, or factual claims without verification. Fabricated sources or unsupported claims are treated as misconduct.

### 6.6 Circumventing Assessment Design
Students may not use AI to bypass the intended learning outcome of an assessment, such as generating answers to assess personal reasoning, analysis, writing, coding, or problem-solving ability.

### 6.7 Impersonation and Deception
Students may not use AI to imitate a human reviewer, source, or classmate, or to conceal plagiarism, source misuse, or identity.

---

# 7. Disclosure and Citation of AI Use
If AI use is allowed in an assignment, students must include a brief statement such as:

> “I used [tool name] to brainstorm ideas and improve grammar. I reviewed and edited all content, and I am responsible for the final submission.”

If the lecturer requires it, students must also provide:
- the prompts used
- the AI outputs relevant to the submission
- a short description of how the output was edited or verified

The university may require a standard AI disclosure template.

---

# 8. Responsibility, Verification, and Sanctions
- Students are responsible for verifying accuracy, originality, and compliance.
- Lecturers may require oral explanation, draft history, process notes, or other evidence of authorship.
- Violations may lead to penalties under the university’s academic misconduct procedures, including resubmission, grade reduction, failure of the assessment, or disciplinary action.

---

# 9. Lecturer’s Right to Set Stricter Rules
Course syllabi, lab manuals, thesis guidelines, and assignment instructions may impose stricter limits than this policy. Where a course says AI is prohibited, that instruction prevails.

---

# 10. Review and Updates
This policy should be reviewed regularly to reflect changes in AI technology, academic practice, legal requirements, and university standards.

---

# How a Lecturer with 200 Students Can Enforce This Policy

A lecturer with 200 students needs a system that is simple, transparent, and scalable. The most effective approach is to combine clear rules, assignment design, disclosure requirements, and selective checking.

## 1. Make the AI rules explicit in every assessment
The lecturer should include a short AI statement in:
- the course syllabus
- each assignment brief
- the LMS page
- exam instructions

Example:
- **Allowed:** brainstorming, grammar checking
- **Not allowed:** generating the final answer
- **Must disclose:** any AI use beyond grammar checking

This reduces confusion and gives the lecturer a clear basis for enforcement.

## 2. Use a tiered AI policy for assignments
Not every task needs the same level of restriction.

### Example structure:
- **No AI allowed:** exams, quizzes, in-class writing, reflections meant to measure personal understanding
- **Limited AI allowed:** essays, reports, code, with disclosure
- **AI encouraged:** optional practice activities, brainstorming, revision support

This helps students know what is acceptable without constant clarification.

## 3. Require a short AI disclosure statement
For every submitted assignment, students can include a small checkbox or 2–3 sentence declaration, such as:
- “No AI tools were used.”
- “AI was used only for grammar checking.”
- “AI was used to generate an outline, which I revised substantially.”

This is easy to collect even for 200 students, especially through an LMS submission form.

## 4. Design assessments that are harder to fake
The lecturer should reduce the usefulness of generic AI-generated answers by:
- asking students to relate answers to class discussions or local Indonesian contexts
- requiring personal reflection tied to course material
- using specific data, case studies, or readings discussed in class
- asking for justification of choices and process, not only final answers
- including drafts, outlines, or progress checkpoints

When students must show their reasoning process, AI misuse becomes easier to detect.

## 5. Use staged submissions
For major assignments, the lecturer can require:
- topic proposal
- outline
- draft
- final submission

This allows comparison across stages and makes sudden shifts in style more visible. It also helps 200 students stay on track.

## 6. Randomly sample students for brief oral checks
A practical enforcement method is to select a small number of students each week or after each assignment for a 3–5 minute verification interview, either in person or online.

Questions can include:
- Why did you choose this argument?
- What does this paragraph mean?
- How did you reach this result?
- Which sources were most important?

Even a small sample creates deterrence. Students know their work may be checked.

## 7. Use draft history and process evidence
For writing and coding assignments, the lecturer can ask for:
- Google Docs version history
- Word track changes
- code commit history
- notes, outlines, or calculations

This is not required for every student all the time, but it is very useful when an submission looks suspicious.

## 8. Screen selectively, not blindly
AI detectors are imperfect and should not be the only basis for punishment. A lecturer with 200 students should use them only as a preliminary signal, not as proof.

Better approach:
- look for unusual changes in tone or complexity
- compare with the student’s previous work
- check whether citations are real and relevant
- ask follow-up questions when needed

## 9. Keep a consistent response process
The lecturer should follow a standard procedure when suspected misuse occurs:
1. Review the submission and disclosure statement
2. Compare with prior work or drafts
3. Invite the student to explain the work process
4. If needed, request supporting evidence
5. Refer confirmed cases to the academic integrity process

This protects fairness and reduces accusations of arbitrary treatment.

## 10. Communicate that integrity is about learning, not punishment
A lecturer will get better compliance if students understand the purpose of the rules:
- to protect fairness
- to ensure grading reflects actual learning
- to build professional responsibility

This is especially important in a large class where anonymous enforcement alone is less effective than a culture of transparency.

---

# Practical Enforcement Model for 200 Students

A workable model could look like this:

### Before the semester
- publish AI rules in syllabus
- explain permitted/restricted/prohibited use in week 1
- give one example of proper AI disclosure
- show one example of misconduct

### During the semester
- use low-stakes practice with allowed AI
- require disclosure for major assignments
- collect drafts or outlines for large tasks
- randomly sample 10–15 students per assignment for oral checks or process review

### At grading stage
- check for missing disclosure statements
- review suspicious cases manually
- compare with prior submissions
- request clarification before alleging misconduct

### If misconduct is confirmed
- apply the university’s academic misconduct procedure
- document the evidence and the student’s explanation
- ensure consistent penalties across students

---

# Short Lecturer Implementation Template

You may want to give lecturers a one-paragraph standard statement like this:

> Students may use AI tools only as permitted in the assignment instructions. Unless otherwise stated, AI may be used for brainstorming and grammar support, but not for generating final answers, code, or analysis. Any AI use beyond basic proofreading must be disclosed in the submission. The lecturer may request drafts, version history, or a brief oral explanation to verify authorship. Undisclosed or unauthorized AI use will be treated as academic misconduct.
